title: Entangled Work Leadership Claydon, Richard
author: Claydon, Richard
summary: Claydon argues that the real organizational pressure is not pace or complexity per se, but the failure of work to sort itself into its distinct types -- what Stefan Norrvall calls the Confusion Tax. Using a three-part framework of Run (continuity work), Serve (integration work), and Change (adaptation work), he describes how organizations routinely load all three onto the same people, forums, and rhythms as if they were one thing. Three failure signatures emerge: Run gets overloaded with what should be Change; Serve becomes invisible (attributed to temperament rather than acknowledged as work); and Change gets misloaded -- arriving wearing impressive language but felt by recipients as more work, more ambiguity, and more responsibility for making senior aspiration locally survivable. The Confusion Tax travels into development conversations, where structural confusion about work becomes feedback about individual resilience, confidence, or maturity. The key diagnostic: when does carrying badly sorted work become leadership, and when does it become the organization rewarding people for absorbing its own incoherence?
points: The Confusion Tax -- the hidden cost of work that has not been clearly distinguished, ranked, or coordinated -- travels into leadership roles and becomes leadership load: the cost of making situations credible upward, workable laterally, and liveable downward simultaneously.

Serve (integration work: translation, repair, expectation management, emotional labor) is chronically invisible -- attributed to personal temperament rather than counted as real work -- which means the system relies on informal repair while pretending formal structures are working as designed.

Change gets misloaded because it arrives wearing better language than Run or Serve, but by the time it reaches people who must carry it, it feels like another workstream, another reporting requirement, and another request to make senior aspiration locally survivable.

Before asking whether people are leading well, leaders should ask whether the work has been distinguished clearly enough to carry -- and before demanding more ownership, should ask whether responsibility, authority, capacity, and design actually line up.

The coordinating middle pays the organization's Confusion Tax: the people close enough to reality to know what is happening and trusted enough to absorb what others would rather not name are the ones being rewarded for absorbing incoherence -- not for leading.
quotes: Stefan Norrvall calls this Confusion Tax: the hidden cost of work that has not been clearly distinguished, ranked, or coordinated.

The visible problem is not always the real problem. In many organisations, the first explanation arrives too quickly. A delay becomes an execution issue. A recurring handoff problem becomes a communication issue. A stakeholder conflict becomes a relationship issue. A tired leader becomes a resilience issue. A confused role becomes a capability gap.

Serve is integration work. It makes the organisation responsive to real contexts. It translates, repairs, adjusts, reassures, interprets, negotiates, and holds interfaces together. It is often undercounted because, when done well, it leaves traces rather than monuments.

People can support the intent of Change and still dread its arrival. That does not automatically make them resistant. It may mean they are experienced enough to know how the future usually enters: as more work, more ambiguity, and more responsibility for making senior aspiration locally survivable.

The organisation may speak as though the work has been allocated. Charts exist. Accountabilities exist. Forums exist. Dashboards exist. Milestones exist. Yet unresolved work keeps arriving at the same human locations: people close enough to reality to know what is happening, senior enough to be expected to do something about it, and trusted enough to absorb the blur.

Before asking whether people are leading well, ask whether the work has been distinguished clearly enough to carry. Before asking for more ownership, ask whether responsibility, authority, capacity, and design line up. Before asking for more resilience, ask what load is being normalised.

Leadership does involve carrying. The answer is not to refuse every burden that is unfair, ambiguous, or under-designed. That would make leadership wonderfully pure and mostly useless. But neither should leadership become the hiding place for work the system refuses to sort.
